title: When Recovery Does Not Move in a Straight Line
script: Narrator: [calm] After a period of illness, my colleague returned to work with a plan that looked sensible on paper: fewer hours, regular breaks, and a review after several weeks.

Narrator: The first difficulty was other people’s expectation that returning meant being fully recovered. On a good day, she could manage a meeting. On another day, the same journey cost far more energy.

Narrator: Her clinician provided individual guidance. The team’s responsibility was not to interpret her condition, but to make the work arrangements clear enough that she could follow that guidance without repeated negotiation.
Narrator: We agreed on priority tasks, a reliable contact person, and a way to say that a limit had been reached without explaining private medical details in a group chat.

Narrator: This was not special treatment. It was an attempt to prevent a predictable problem: a person who tries to appear fine may push beyond a sensible pace because every request feels like a test of commitment.

Narrator: The arrangement was reviewed rather than frozen. Some adjustments became unnecessary; others needed to continue. The important point was that change did not have to be defended as a moral failure.
Narrator: I learned to avoid cheerful but unhelpful comments such as, You look much better, as if appearance settled the question of capacity.
Narrator: More useful questions were practical: Which part of the day is hardest? Would a written summary help? Is there a task that can wait?

Narrator: No friend or manager should promise a medical outcome. But we can reduce needless pressure, respect privacy, and encourage someone to seek appropriate help if symptoms change or become urgent.
Narrator: Recovery is personal, but it is never only personal. Workplaces and families can either make a careful plan possible or quietly make it much harder to follow.
